title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Je me lève à + num + heures

rules.text: French has ONE present and it covers both of English's. Je mange is "I eat" AND "I am eating" — the same three words — and which one it is comes from the sentence around it, never from the verb.

There is no continuous to build, so there is nothing to translate the -ing with. Je suis manger is two verbs with nothing joining them, and it is what an English speaker assembles when they go looking for the missing form.

Daily verbs carry a little pronoun that is part of the verb and changes with the person: je me lève · vous vous levez. English "I get up" has nothing at all standing where me stands, so leaving it out is the commonest slip in the module.

The -er present across the persons this course writes: je mange · vous mangez · il/elle mange. Three of those endings are SILENT — mange, manges and mangent are one sound — so the subject pronoun is what carries the person to the ear, and French can never drop it.

Time goes in front of the clause or at its end, and the definite article is what turns a day into a habit: le matin is "in the morning", every morning, and le lundi is "on Mondays", while lundi on its own is one particular Monday.

The clock is à + a number + heures, and heures is written plural from two upwards: à sept heures, but à une heure. English hangs "o'clock" on the end; French puts the word for hour in the middle and never leaves it out.
An article cannot sit on its own vowel next to another: le eau is impossible, so le and la shorten to l' and weld onto the noun — l'eau. The partitive does the same: de la eau becomes de l'eau.
Negation still wraps the verb exactly as L1-M3 taught it, whatever else the sentence carries: Le soir je ne travaille pas.

words.note: manger with a person on it: je mange · vous mangez · il/elle mange. One present covers both of English's — "I eat" and "I am eating" — and je mange and il mange sound alike, so the pronoun never goes.
Here it is the "at" of a time — à sept heures. In L1-M7 it is the "at" or "to" of a place — à la maison, au marché. The accent is the whole difference from a ("has"): never left off.
seven. The p is silent — set — and the final -t is sounded, which is unusual enough to be worth remembering. Numbers as a set are L1-M8's; this one is here because the clock needs it.
hour. The h is silent, so sept heures runs together as set-UR. It is written plural from two upwards — à sept heures, but à une heure — and it is never left out: French has no bare "at seven".

sentences.trap: English can say "I eat at seven" and stop. French cannot: heures is part of the time, not an optional flourish, so à sept is not a time at all.
sentences.sound: mahnzh, with the an nasal and the final -e silent. sept is set — the p says nothing. The h of heures is silent too, so the two words run together: set-UR.

variations.display: Je mange à une heure
variations.changed: one o'clock takes the singular heure — the plural starts at two

variations.display: Vous mangez à sept heures ?
variations.changed: mangez for the person you are speaking to, asked with a rising voice

variations.display: Je ne mange pas à sept heures
variations.changed: L1-M3's brackets close around the verb; the time phrase stays outside them

mistake.display: Je suis manger à sept heures
mistake.why: There is no continuous to assemble: je mange already means "I am eating". Putting suis in front leaves two verbs with nothing joining them.

sentences.usage: Saying when you do something, every day.
sentences.mnemonic: French counts the hours out loud: seven hours, not seven o'clock.

sentences.display: Je me lève à sept heures
sentences.cue: I get up at seven o'clock

words.note: se lever, "to raise oneself". The little pronoun is part of the verb and changes with the person: je me lève · vous vous levez. lève carries a grave accent and levez does not.

sentences.trap: English "I get up" has nothing standing where me stands, so an English speaker drops it and writes Je lève — which means "I raise" something else, and leaves the sentence waiting for an object.
sentences.sound: muh LEV, with the è an open eh sound the grave accent marks. In vous vous levez the two vous are said identically and both are needed.

variations.display: Vous vous levez à sept heures ?
variations.cue: Do you get up at seven?
variations.changed: both vous — the subject and the verb's own pronoun — and the accent goes with the ending

variations.display: Je me lève à une heure
variations.cue: I get up at one o'clock
variations.changed: swap the hour; heure goes singular at one

variations.display: Le lundi je me lève à sept heures
variations.cue: On Mondays I get up at seven
variations.changed: a habit word in front — and the rest of the sentence does not move

mistake.why: Without me the verb is "I raise", and the sentence is left waiting to hear what. Getting yourself up is je me lève.

sentences.usage: The first thing anyone says about their day.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not just get up in French — you raise yourself.

sentences.display: Le matin je mange du pain
sentences.cue: In the morning I eat bread

words.note: in the morning — and, said this way, every morning. French uses the definite article where English uses "in the", and the article is what makes it a habit rather than one particular morning.

sentences.trap: English marks a habit with a word like "usually" or with nothing at all. French marks it with le, quietly, in front of the time word — and a learner who leaves the le off has written something that means one specific morning.
sentences.sound: luh ma-TAN, with the in nasal and the n never sounded on its own.

variations.display: Le matin je bois du café
variations.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
variations.changed: swap the habit — the time phrase does not move

variations.display: Je mange du pain le matin
variations.cue: I eat bread in the morning
variations.changed: the time phrase goes to the end just as happily; nothing else changes

variations.display: Le matin je ne mange pas
variations.cue: In the morning I don't eat
variations.changed: the brackets close round the verb, with the time phrase outside them

mistake.display: En le matin je mange du pain
mistake.why: There is no word for "in" here: le matin already carries it. En le is not French in any case — that pair does not exist.

sentences.usage: Describing what you habitually do at a time of day.
sentences.mnemonic: le is the habit marker: THE morning means every morning.

words.note: on Mondays — every Monday. The article is what makes it a habit: lundi alone is one particular Monday, usually the next. Days of the week are lowercase in French.
travailler with a person on it: je travaille · vous travaillez. The bare form travailler was L1-M3's; this is the same verb doing the sentence's own work rather than following another verb.

sentences.trap: English needs a plural and a preposition to say this — "on MondayS". French needs neither: one singular day with le in front of it is the whole habit.
sentences.sound: luh luhn-DEE, with the un nasal. travaille is tra-VAI — the ill is a y as in "yes", never an l sound.

variations.display: Le lundi je ne travaille pas
variations.changed: the brackets round the verb, with the day left outside

variations.display: Vous travaillez le lundi ?
variations.changed: travaillez, a rising voice, and the day moved to the end

variations.display: Le matin je travaille
variations.changed: swap one habit phrase for another; both are built the same way

mistake.why: Days of the week are lowercase in French. The capital is English showing through, and it is the one difference the eye catches immediately.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do on a given day, week after week.
sentences.mnemonic: One day plus le makes all of them.

words.note: every day — literally "all the days", and French says it in the plural where English says it in the singular. Take the three words together: they are a fixed phrase, and the -s of tous is silent here.

sentences.trap: "Every day" is singular in English and plural in French, so the word-for-word translation goes wrong in both halves at once: there is no French chaque jour in everyday speech about routine, and there is no singular in this phrase at all.
sentences.sound: too lay ZHOOR. The -s of tous is silent when it sits in front of a noun like this, and the -s of jours is silent as always.

variations.display: Je mange à sept heures tous les jours
variations.cue: I eat at seven every day
variations.changed: the phrase goes at the very end, after the time

variations.display: Vous travaillez tous les jours ?
variations.changed: travaillez and a rising voice; the phrase is untouched

variations.display: Je ne travaille pas tous les jours
variations.changed: the brackets close round the verb and the phrase stays outside

mistake.why: That is "all day long", a different thing entirely. The routine phrase is plural: tous les jours.

sentences.usage: Saying how often — the plainest habit word there is.
sentences.mnemonic: French counts them: all the days, not every day.

words.note: at what time. quelle is "which" and agrees with feminine heure, so the two l's and the -e are not optional. In speech it often stays at the end: Vous mangez à quelle heure ?

sentences.trap: English hauls the whole question to the front and inserts a "do": "What time DO you eat?". French leaves the sentence standing and puts the question phrase where the answer would go.
sentences.sound: a KEL-ur. The l of quelle links straight into the silent h of heure, so the last two words sound like one.

variations.display: Vous vous levez à quelle heure ?
variations.cue: What time do you get up?
variations.changed: swap the verb — the question phrase does not move

variations.display: À quelle heure vous mangez ?
variations.changed: the phrase moved to the front instead; still nothing inverted

variations.display: Je mange à sept heures
variations.changed: the answer — the time takes exactly the seat the question phrase held

mistake.why: heure is feminine, so it is quelle with two l's and an -e. quel would be agreeing with a masculine noun that is not there.

sentences.mnemonic: Put the question where the answer will go, and move nothing.

sentences.display: Je bois du café le matin
sentences.cue: I drink coffee in the morning

words.note: boire with a person on it, irregular enough to learn whole: je bois · vous buvez. The stem itself changes, which -er verbs never do — compare je mange · vous mangez, where only the ending moved.

sentences.trap: The partitive is still there under the habit: it is coffee in general, so du café, exactly as in L1-M3. A time phrase never takes an article away.
sentences.sound: bwa, one syllable, with the final -s silent. buvez is bü-VAY — a different stem, and the ending sounds like every other -ez.

variations.display: Vous buvez du café le matin ?
variations.cue: Do you drink coffee in the morning?
variations.changed: buvez — the stem changes, not just the ending — and a rising voice

variations.display: Le matin je bois du thé
variations.cue: In the morning I drink tea
variations.changed: the time phrase to the front and another mass noun behind the verb

variations.display: Je ne bois pas de café
variations.changed: the brackets round the verb, and du collapses to a bare de behind them

mistake.why: The partitive does not vanish because a time word turned up: du café, as it was in L1-M3.

sentences.usage: A habit with a thing in it — the ordinary shape of talking about your day.
sentences.mnemonic: -er verbs change their ending; boire changes its middle.

sentences.display: Le soir je ne travaille pas
sentences.cue: In the evening I don't work

words.note: in the evening — every evening, by the same article that made le matin a habit. It is the third of this module's fixed time phrases, and like the others it is taken whole.

sentences.trap: The negation and the time phrase never interfere with each other. The brackets go round the verb only, so le soir stands entirely outside them, at the front or at the end.
sentences.sound: luh SWAR, one syllable after the article, with the r in the back of the throat.

variations.display: Le soir je mange à la maison
variations.cue: In the evening I eat at home
variations.changed: a positive habit in the same time frame

variations.display: Je ne travaille pas le soir
variations.cue: I don't work in the evening
variations.changed: the time phrase to the end — the brackets do not move with it

variations.display: Vous ne travaillez pas le soir ?
variations.cue: Don't you work in the evening?
variations.changed: travaillez inside the same brackets, asked with a rising voice

mistake.display: Le soir je ne pas travaille
mistake.why: pas goes AFTER the verb, not in front of it: je ne travaille pas. The two halves are brackets, and the verb sits between them.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do not do, at a time of day.
sentences.mnemonic: Time outside the brackets, verb inside.

words.note: house — feminine, so la maison. With à in front of it, à la maison is how French says "at home": there is no separate word for home in this sense, and the article is not optional.

sentences.trap: English "at home" has no article in it at all. French keeps la, so à la maison is the phrase — and the à here is the same à that told the time in S01, doing the other of its two jobs.
sentences.sound: meh-ZOHN, with the s between two vowels sounding like a z and the on nasal.

variations.display: Le soir je mange à la maison
variations.cue: In the evening I eat at home
variations.changed: a habit phrase in front — the place phrase does not move

variations.display: Vous mangez à la maison ?
variations.changed: mangez and a rising voice

variations.display: Je travaille à la maison
variations.changed: swap the verb — à la maison is the frame

mistake.why: The article stays: à la maison. Dropping it is English's "at home" arriving whole.

sentences.usage: Saying where you do something — the first place phrase of the course.
sentences.mnemonic: French eats at THE house; only English can eat at home.

words.note: water. eau is feminine, so it should be la eau — but an article cannot sit on its own vowel next to another, so la shortens to l': l'eau. The partitive does the same: de l'eau.

sentences.trap: The article did not disappear — it shrank. A learner who reads l'eau as a bare noun will write le eau or la eau later, and neither is a spelling French allows.
sentences.sound: duh LOH. The eau spelling is one plain o sound, and the l runs straight into it with nothing in between.

variations.display: Je veux de l'eau
variations.changed: L1-M3's verb with the same welded article behind it

variations.display: Vous buvez de l'eau ?
variations.changed: buvez and a rising voice; the welding is unaffected

variations.display: Je ne bois pas d'eau
variations.changed: behind the negation the partitive collapses to de — and de shortens too, to d'

mistake.why: Two vowels cannot sit side by side across an article: la becomes l' and welds on. It is de l'eau.

sentences.usage: Everyday drinking — and the first place the course shows an article shrinking.
sentences.mnemonic: French will not let two vowels collide: the article gives up its own.
